findings: Rare isolated premature ventricular complexes (under 1% burden), benign. No sustained arrhythmia, no pauses greater than 2 seconds, no AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.impression: 24-hour Holter monitor with only benign findings.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Predominant sinus rhythm throughout the recording

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

citations: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Intermittent convergence with miosis on lateral gaze, normal motility and full ductions between episodes
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The examination makes the diagnosis: convergence spasm with miosis, coming and going with normal motility and full ductions, is the positive sign of functional diplopia, and it separates near-reflex spasm from a sixth nerve palsy or a decompensated strabismus.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No brainstem, posterior fossa or craniocervical lesion; one tiny nonspecific frontal focus
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI before accepting convergence spasm
action_criteria.rationale: An acquired esotropia can rarely come from a brainstem or posterior fossa lesion, including a Chiari malformation, so one non-contrast MRI is advised before the spasm is accepted as functional. No gadolinium is needed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Low-risk SSRI-triptan pairing; sulfonamide allergy not relevant to sumatriptan in practice
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Sertraline with occasional sumatriptan is a low-risk serotonergic pair; nothing in the list affects the eyes or changes the plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway (criteria pack, optional tier).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it (round ruling 5).

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Offer strabismus surgery for the convergence spasm.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional diplopia with convergence spasm) based on intermittent convergence spasm with miosis and full ductions between episodes, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, give written information, and address her concern about multiple sclerosis.
Arrange orthoptic assessment and convergence-relaxation exercises.

avoided_actions.rationale: Her palpitations and chest tightness had a negative cardiac work-up and do not bear on the diplopia.
Intermittent palpitations with a prior negative cardiac work-up and no syncope; a rhythm recording answers no question about the diplopia.
CT images the posterior fossa poorly; the MRI answers the structural question.
No papilledema, headache or meningism; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
FDG-PET has no role in diplopia with convergence spasm.
No limb weakness or sensory deficit; EMG and nerve conduction studies answer no question.
Midline splitting of vibration is a nonspecific functional feature, not a pathway lesion; evoked potentials answer no question.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with functional diplopia due to convergence spasm

differential.diagnosis: Acute acquired comitant esotropia or decompensated childhood strabismus
differential.key_features: Prior bilateral medial rectus recession and 10-12 hours a day of screen use favour it, but the esotropia comes and goes with miosis and accommodative effort, and alignment is normal between episodes.
Full ductions, a comitant deviation, miosis during the apparent abduction failure and no papilledema argue against it.
Variable diplopia worse with fatigue raises it, but there is no ptosis, ductions are full, and the pupil constricts with the deviation, which myasthenia never does.

differential.diagnosis: Brainstem or posterior fossa lesion, including Chiari malformation
differential.key_features: These can cause acquired esotropia or near-reflex spasm; the MRI shows a normal brainstem, cerebellum and craniocervical junction.
Raised by a maternal aunt with MS and the MRI focus, but a single 3 mm nonspecific subcortical focus does not meet dissemination in space, and there is no brainstem lesion to explain the diplopia.

key_clinical_evidence: Convergence spasm with miosis and accommodative effort on lateral gaze, alternating with entirely normal ocular motility.
Comitant esotropia of 25-30 prism diopters at distance during episodes, full ductions, and a Hess chart abnormal during an episode and normal 20 minutes later.
Non-contrast MRI shows no brainstem, posterior fossa or craniocervical lesion; a single 3 mm subcortical focus is nonspecific.
Childhood strabismus surgery and heavy screen use raise decompensated strabismus, which does not produce miosis or normal alignment between episodes.
Recent divorce and work stress are context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with MS barely changes her risk; the diplopia has a positive functional sign and no brainstem lesion.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on MS and pursuing gadolinium MRI, spinal imaging or a lumbar puncture

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A solitary punctate subcortical focus is a common nonspecific finding, does not meet dissemination in space and cannot cause the diplopia.
red_herrings.data_point: Single 3 mm right frontal subcortical T2/FLAIR focus
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reading the focus as demyelination and escalating investigation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neither explains miosis with the deviation or normal alignment between episodes; the pattern is convergence spasm.
red_herrings.data_point: Childhood bilateral medial rectus recession and 10-12 hours of daily screen time
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnosing decompensated strabismus or screen-related esotropia and referring for surgery
red_herrings.location: Past medical history and social history

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; convergence spasm with miosis is the positive sign.
red_herrings.data_point: Adjustment disorder with anxiety on sertraline
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a psychological label without the positive sign, or dismissing the diplopia because she is anxious

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: On sustained lateral gaze, intermittent bilateral convergence with pupillary constriction and accommodative effort, alternating with periods of entirely normal ocular motility.

Comitant esotropia of 25-30 prism diopters at distance during episodes and normal alignment between them; full ductions; Hess chart showing inward displacement of both eyes during an episode and normal 20 minutes later.
Visual acuity 20/20 in each eye with correction, normal fundi without papilledema, no nystagmus, no ptosis.
Midline splitting of vibration sense on the forehead; not counted as a rule-in sign.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive sign of functional diplopia: convergence spasm with miosis, intermittent and variable, with full ductions between episodes. The pattern is inconsistent with a cranial nerve palsy or a structural lesion.

interactions: Sertraline + sumatriptan: additive serotonergic effect; serotonin syndrome is rare at these doses. Counsel on agitation, tremor, hyperthermia and clonus.
general.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed, approximately twice monthly; Melatonin 3 mg nightly
general.summary: One interaction of low clinical risk: sertraline with sumatriptan (serotonergic). No interaction with melatonin.
warnings: Sulfonamide allergy (rash): sumatriptan contains a non-antibiotic sulfonamide group; cross-reactivity is unlikely, and she already tolerates it.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI without intravenous contrast, with thin sections through the brainstem.
Normal brainstem, cerebellum and craniocervical junction; cerebellar tonsils in normal position.
Cisternal segments of cranial nerves III, IV and VI normal in course and caliber.
No periventricular, juxtacortical or infratentorial lesion. Normal ventricles.
mri.impression: 1. Single 3 mm nonspecific T2/FLAIR hyperintense focus in the right frontal subcortical white matter, without restricted diffusion. 2. No brainstem or posterior fossa lesion; no mass, hemorrhage or hydrocephalus.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to several confounders: childhood strabismus surgery suggesting recurrence, high screen time suggesting device-related acquired esotropia, a nonspecific white matter focus raising MS concern, and a family history of MS. Convergence spasm with miosis is the positive sign, and it needs neuro-ophthalmological reasoning to recognise.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional diplopia: the agent must recognise convergence spasm with miosis as the positive sign, obtain one non-contrast MRI, and not be drawn into MS or strabismus work-up by the family history, the incidental focus or the childhood surgery.

patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old right-handed woman presents to the neurology inpatient service after referral from ophthalmology for evaluation of acute-onset horizontal diplopia. The patient reports that approximately 3 weeks ago, she began noticing double vision when looking at distant objects, particularly when watching television or looking across a room. The diplopia is described as horizontal, with images side by side, and resolves completely when she covers either eye. She notes the symptoms are intermittent and seem to worsen during periods of stress or fatigue, and she has noticed improvement on weekends when she is more relaxed. Near vision activities such as reading on her phone or computer do not provoke diplopia. She denies any associated headache, nausea, vomiting, or change in vision clarity. There is no history of recent head trauma, febrile illness, or new medications. She reports increased daily screen time over the past several months due to remote work, averaging 10 to 12 hours per day on digital devices. The patient was initially evaluated by ophthalmology, who documented intermittent comitant esotropia of 25 to 30 prism diopters at distance and variable measurements at near, with full ocular ductions and no nystagmus. The ophthalmologist noted that the esotropia was inconsistently present during different portions of the examination, with periods of normal alignment. Given her childhood history of strabismus surgery and the acute presentation, she was referred to neurology to exclude intracranial pathology. The patient reports significant psychosocial stress over the past year, including a difficult divorce, workplace instability, and estrangement from a family member. She endorses poor sleep quality with early morning awakenings and intermittent episodes of palpitations and chest tightness over the past several months. She has a maternal aunt diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, which has been causing her considerable anxiety about her own neurological health.

neurological_exam.additional: Convergence spasm observed intermittently during extraocular movement testing: episodes of bilateral eye convergence with miosis, followed by periods of entirely normal ocular motility. Ophthalmology measured a comitant esotropia of 25-30 prism diopters during episodes, with alignment normalizing spontaneously. Hess red-green testing during an episode showed inward displacement of both eyes with equal field sizes; testing repeated 20 minutes later was normal.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN I: not tested. CN II: visual acuity 20/20 OU with correction. Visual fields full to confrontation. Funduscopic exam normal bilaterally, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: intermittent convergent eye deviation noted, inconsistently present during examination; at times eyes track smoothly in all directions without restriction, with full abduction of each eye between episodes. During sustained lateral gaze testing, patient intermittently develops convergence spasm with pupillary constriction and accommodative effort. Bell reflex present and normal bilaterally. CN V: sensation intact V1-V3 bilaterally. CN VII: symmetric face. CN VIII: hearing grossly intact. CN IX/X: palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal base, normal stride length, tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Mildly anxious affect. Speech fluent without dysarthria. Follows complex commands. Recall 3/3 at 5 minutes. No evidence of cognitive impairment on bedside testing.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone normal in all extremities. Bulk normal. Strength 5/5 throughout bilateral upper and lower extremities with consistent effort. No drift on pronator testing. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities. Midline splitting of vibration sense noted on forehead testing (non-anatomic pattern).
